title: Benchmarking LLM Inference at Scale with AIPerf | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA has replaced GenAI-Perf with AIPerf, a ground-up multiprocess rewrite built so the load client stops being the measurement bottleneck under high concurrency, coordinated over ZMQ with separate worker and record-processor services. The walkthrough exposes two benchmarking traps that silently corrupt published LLM throughput numbers - omitting min_tokens and ignore_eos lets models stop early and understates throughput, and running without --streaming makes TTFT and ITL unmeasurable - and shows that single-concurrency runs produce the lowest possible TTFT at the cost of throughput. Acknowledgments name engineers at AWS, Coreweave, Baseten and Pinterest collaborating to standardize on AIPerf.

themes.theme: Client-side bottleneck as the hidden measurement error

insights.claim: NVIDIA AIPerf is the designated successor to GenAI-Perf and a ground-up rewrite that no longer runs on top of Perf Analyzer, a clean architectural break that NVIDIA says is the reason it can scale.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: GenAI-Perf-based numbers in existing vendor comparisons come from a deprecated architecture; expect a wave of restated inference benchmarks as teams migrate.
insights.quote: AIPerf is the designated successor to GenAI-Perf and is a ground-up rewrite.
insights.locator: What AIPerf does differently

insights.claim: Most LLM load generators, including GenAI-Perf itself, use a single-process architecture that becomes GIL-bound under real concurrency or request rate, meaning the benchmark client rather than the inference server sets the measured ceiling.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: A large share of published LLM serving throughput figures may be measuring the test harness, not the hardware or the serving stack - a reason to distrust cross-vendor inference comparisons.
insights.quote: Most benchmarkers, GenAI-Perf included, use a single-process architecture that becomes GIL-bound under real concurrency or request rate.
insights.locator: The client shouldn't be the bottleneck

insights.claim: AIPerf splits benchmarking into worker processes that generate load and separate record-processor services that handle results, coordinated over ZMQ, specifically to keep the client from capping measured server performance.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: The architectural tell of a trustworthy load generator is process separation between generation and record processing; use it to screen any benchmarking tool.
insights.quote: worker processes generate load, separate record-processor services handle results, and everything is coordinated over ZMQ
insights.locator: The client shouldn't be the bottleneck

insights.claim: The alternatives engineers typically reach for - curl commands, hand-rolled asyncio scripts, or one-off load generators - all share single-process performance limits and produce results measured against a self-built reference, so the numbers cannot be fully trusted.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Internal inference performance claims built on bespoke scripts should be treated as unvalidated until reproduced on a multiprocess harness.
insights.quote: you end up with results you can’t fully trust, attached to tooling you’ll have to rewrite the moment requirements change
insights.locator: You're deploying a model on a system

themes.theme: Configuration traps that corrupt published numbers

insights.claim: Without the flags --extra-inputs min_tokens:128 and --extra-inputs ignore_eos:true, the requested output token count is only a suggestion because the model stops whenever it naturally finishes, so measured throughput ends up lower than it should be and is not reproducible across runs.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Benchmarks that omit EOS suppression systematically understate tokens/sec and vary run to run - the single most checkable flaw in a competitor's inference numbers.
insights.quote: Without these, the output token count is a suggestion.
insights.locator: Running the benchmark

insights.claim: Streaming mode is mandatory for measuring time-to-first-token and inter-token latency, because without it the server batches the full response before sending and there are no first- or decode-token events to observe at all.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Any latency claim citing TTFT from a non-streaming run is fabricated by construction; verify the streaming flag before accepting interactive-latency comparisons.
insights.quote: --streaming is not optional if you want to measure TTFT and ITL.
insights.locator: Running the benchmark

insights.claim: Pinning both synthetic input and output token standard deviations to zero at 128 tokens each reproduces the commonly used static benchmark that holds request and output lengths constant, which the author frames as a clean baseline rather than a realistic workload.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: The industry-standard 128/128 static benchmark is explicitly an idealized reference point, not a production proxy - discount headline numbers derived from it.
insights.quote: This reproduces a commonly used static benchmark that holds request and output lengths constant.
insights.locator: A few flags here are doing more work

insights.claim: Setting --random-seed 42 makes Poisson arrival timing and synthetic length draws reproducible so that rerunning the same command produces the same sequence of requests.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Seeded arrival patterns turn stochastic load tests into repeatable A/B comparisons across serving stacks and hardware generations.
insights.quote: --random-seed 42 makes the Poisson timing and synthetic length draws reproducible.
insights.locator: Going further: Configuring a traffic pattern

insights.claim: On aarch64 the crick dependency ships as source-only and requires a C toolchain such as build-essential on Debian or Ubuntu and Development Tools on RHEL, which is why AIPerf installs can stall on that package.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Arm-based inference deployments hit a friction point in NVIDIA's own tooling chain, a small signal on the maturity gap between x86 and Arm AI stacks.
insights.quote: on aarch64, the crick dependency ships as source-only and requires a C toolchain
insights.locator: Install AIPerf

themes.theme: Metrics that actually diagnose serving stacks

insights.claim: AIPerf's core four metrics are TTFT as the primary latency signal for interactive use, ITL for decode-phase health, request latency combining prefill and decode into one number, and output token throughput as the primary throughput signal for capacity planning.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Separating prefill-bound from decode-bound problems determines whether more compute or more memory bandwidth fixes a serving bottleneck - a direct hardware-spend decision.
insights.quote: High ITL means the decode phase is struggling, even if TTFT looks healthy.
insights.locator: Reading the numbers: What AIPerf surfaces

insights.claim: Each core metric is reported at p25, p50, p75, p90, p95 and p99 alongside minimum, maximum, average and standard deviation, because a server with a healthy mean TTFT and an outlier p99 looks fine in aggregate and fails in production.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Mean-only latency reporting hides the tail that determines real user experience and SLA breaches; insist on p99 in any inference vendor comparison.
insights.quote: a server with a healthy mean TTFT and an outlier p99 looks fine in aggregate and fails in production
insights.locator: Getting the full picture

insights.claim: With DCGM or pynvml available, AIPerf pulls GPU power draw, utilization and memory consumption into the same run output, so correlating a latency spike with a memory pressure event no longer requires a separate profiling session.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Joint latency and power telemetry in one run makes tokens-per-watt and tokens-per-dollar analysis routine, which is the metric that increasingly drives datacenter buying.
insights.quote: AIPerf also pulls GPU power draw, utilization, and memory consumption into the same run output
insights.locator: Beyond the core four

insights.claim: Switching to a Poisson arrival pattern at 10 requests per second draws inter-arrival times from an exponential distribution so the server experiences bursts and gaps rather than a single user stream, which is what queuing actually looks like under real traffic.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Constant-rate benchmarks systematically omit queueing effects, so capacity plans built on them under-provision for real bursty traffic.
insights.quote: The server now experiences bursts and gaps rather than a single user stream, which is what queuing actually looks like under real traffic.
insights.locator: Going further: Configuring a traffic pattern

insights.claim: In the Poisson run with a 512-token input mean and 128-token standard deviation, realized input sequence lengths ranged from 154 to 818 tokens, and the resulting metric distributions were noticeably wider than the static baseline.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Prompt-length variance alone spreads prefill cost across a 5x range, which is why fixed-ISL benchmarks overstate predictability of serving performance.
insights.quote: with input sequence lengths ranging 154 to 818 tokens
insights.locator: You can see in Figure 5

insights.claim: A single-concurrency benchmark is an idealized scenario running one request at a time that presents the lowest possible time-to-first-token at the cost of throughput, while the Poisson run showed a much wider TTFT spread as requests competed for GPU access and prefill and decode overlapped.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Latency numbers quoted at concurrency 1 are a best case that no loaded production server reproduces - a standard way inference marketing flatters itself.
insights.quote: The single-concurrency case is an idealized scenario which runs one request at a time presenting the lowest possible TTFT, at the cost of throughput.
insights.locator: Comparing TTFT between the two runs

insights.claim: AIPerf supports more than 15 endpoint types including chat, responses, NIM rankings and image generation, plus public datasets like ShareGPT and trace replay formats from Mooncake, Baseten and WEKA AgentX, so synthetic smoke tests and replayed production traffic use the same tool.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Native trace-replay support for third-party inference providers' formats signals NVIDIA is positioning AIPerf as the neutral industry measurement layer, not just a CUDA-stack tool.
insights.quote: AIPerf supports 15+ endpoint types: chat, responses, NIM rankings, image generation, and more
insights.locator: Workload breadth that matches what you actually run

insights.claim: AIPerf exposes constant, Poisson and gamma arrival patterns with tunable burstiness, gradual ramping for concurrency and request rate, and synthetic distributions including the vLLM/SGLang range-ratio for variable input and output sequence lengths.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Controlling load shape rather than only volume is what separates a capacity model from a marketing number when sizing inference fleets.
insights.quote: AIPerf supports constant, Poisson, and gamma arrival patterns with tunable burstiness
insights.locator: Load shape you actually control

insights.claim: AIPerf's acknowledgments credit Loki Ravi, Dan Ferguson and Sheng Moua of AWS for cross-company validation and efforts to standardize on AIPerf, Aaron Batilo of Coreweave for the Weights & Biases exporter and sweep reliability work, Shounak Ray and Michael Feil of Baseten for trace replay support, and Cristian Lopez of Pinterest for DAG benchmarking methodology.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Rival clouds and neoclouds contributing to NVIDIA's benchmark tool means NVIDIA is capturing the definition of how inference performance is measured across the industry - durable soft power beyond silicon.
insights.quote: AIPerf is a collaborative effort between NVIDIA and external contributors.
insights.locator: Acknowledgments

insights.claim: The same AIPerf tool is built to handle multi-node Kubernetes deployments, KV cache reuse warm-up mechanics, trace replay from production traffic, prefix synthesis, custom datasets and sweep configurations across concurrency levels.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: KV-cache-reuse and prefix-synthesis benchmarking becoming standard features indicates cache hit rate is now a first-class economic variable in inference serving.
insights.quote: The same tool handles multi-node Kubernetes deployments, KV cache reuse warm up mechanics, trace replay from production traffic, prefix synthesis, custom datasets, and sweep configurations across concurrency levels.
insights.locator: There's more to explore

insights.claim: The walkthrough deliberately uses Qwen3-0.6B served through vLLM because it is small enough for a single GPU and fast enough to iterate on, with the stated point being to establish a measurement loop where swapping the model or endpoint is a one-flag change.
insights.speaker: Francesco Di Natale
insights.so_what: Benchmark tooling that abstracts the model behind a flag lowers the switching cost between serving stacks, which erodes lock-in for individual inference vendors.
insights.quote: The point isn’t to benchmark Qwen3-0.6B specifically; it’s to establish the measurement loop.
insights.locator: Your maiden benchmark: Synthetic ISL/OSL on vLLM
